extracted.intended_audience: student reporters / journalism students / aspiring newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria from a journalism textbook on what makes material newsworthy and how reporters should gather, verify, and write stories. Covers requisites for reporting, many specific news-value dimensions, verification, concision, editorial policy, and usage/style rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic and intelligent interest in people and events
rubrics_metrics.description: First requisite for successful reporting: a sympathetic and intelligent interest in people and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter must be intensely human and sincerely interested in people and events; this interest helps select stories that will appeal to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of where stories may be found and willingness to work hard
rubrics_metrics.description: Second requisite: knowledge of where stories may be found and willingness to work hard to find them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes indefatigable effort to learn unfamiliar subjects (example: reporter spending five hours in library to understand a technical interview) rather than imposing on sources for definitions; industrious reporting yields better, publishable stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to distinguish news and drive it out of the commonplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Third requisite: the ability to distinguish news and drive it out of the covert of the commonplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter must seek significance in events, not get lost in technical details; sees everything as copy or not copy and finds the 'feature' that makes an ordinary incident newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to write rapidly, accurately, and interestingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth requisite: the power to write rapidly, accurately, and interestingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporter should be able to write quickly while maintaining accuracy and readability; avoid 'cut-and-dried' writing and aim to supply interest by method of treatment when facts are not themselves curious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to estimate the relative values of news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth requisite: ability to estimate relative values of stories and avoid wasting time on trivial items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed by introspection and being representative of the readership; reporters should intuitively know how much 'play' a story merits and prioritize accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explanations clear to the average reader (newspaper instinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge alone is not enough; the reporter needs the 'newspaper instinct' to make readers understand explanations and avoid overemphasis on theory or technical intricacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great scholar may fail as a reporter if unable to simplify; focus on facts that can be passed to the public in a bright and interesting story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy Always
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is the first essential of a news story. Without it an intriguing narrative is valueless as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers must check and counter-check facts, avoid coloring or distortion, and be fair in presenting both sides; the slogan 'Accuracy Always' should be a reporter's watchword.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter must check every point
rubrics_metrics.description: No story is news that is not absolutely accurate; the reporter must never turn in a story until he has satisfied himself by conscientious checking that he has told nothing but facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is non-negotiable: reporters who 'fake' lose credibility and livelihood; speed must never compromise verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest (as a news value)
rubrics_metrics.description: After accuracy, the reporter should look for elements of interest in a story; if facts are not curious or unusual, interest must be supplied by treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter who enjoys his work will avoid formulaic writing and make stories readable; identify what will excite curiosity or provoke thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of two events of equal importance, the more recent has the greater news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should seek the 'very latest' developments and work with speed consistent with accuracy; timeliness is a primary requisite alongside accuracy and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unusual (unusualness)
rubrics_metrics.description: People are interested in unusual, extreme, bizarre, or extraordinary experiences; the unusual gives news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a morbid pursuit of sensationalism, but a recognition that glimpses of life 'out there' attract readers; reputable papers play up the different or extraordinary features they record.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected elements or twists often make ordinary events into newsworthy stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a wedding turned front-page because of an accident and the groom proceeding despite injury; unexpected complications or coincidences increase play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features found everywhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story, no matter how insignificant, has a point of attack or a little feature that distinguishes it from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clever reporter can find interesting facts in commonplace incidents — look for unusual aspects in circumstances, persons, places, time, coincidences, or complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contests and records
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of contests or records often have great news value because audiences like accounts of competition and achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize action and struggle; even unusual records (e.g., skinning fish) can receive front-page play due to public interest in winners and achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearness or connection to the reader's home lends news value; people pay more attention to happenings in their own town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including elements of local interest improves a story's appeal for a home paper; famous people visiting or events linked to the reader's locale increase prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that arouse pity, sympathy, romance, or humor have news value by appealing to common human emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pathos sparingly (without overdoing it); items about helpless people, children, animals, romance, and humor attract readers especially around holidays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of life or property
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of deaths, injuries, or property destruction have high news value and are often summarized with boxed lists to lead stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence correlates with numbers killed/injured or value of property destroyed; newspapers respond to public demand for information on misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big names (celebrities / notorious persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving famous or notorious people have greater news value and draw widespread reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A celebrity's minor indisposition can become national news; publications cover what the public wishes to know about public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big events and public issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Important public projects or issues (e.g., reclamation projects, prohibition enforcement) command reader interest even for routine notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale or historically significant events attract continuous attention in the relevant region or nationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known places
rubrics_metrics.description: Events occurring at famous or historic places gain news value from their setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference to a historic place (e.g., Faneuil Hall) can add a readability-enhancing touch and increase interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal interest (seven appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that appeal to basic personal interests — self-preservation, love of home and family, property, ambition for power, longing for reputation, patriotism, and gratification of tastes — increase engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The greater the number of these appeals a story makes, the greater its personal interest; use these appeals to evaluate and shape stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories of definite appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular story types hold definite audiences: medical discoveries for the ailing, housing or money-making opportunities for families, achievements in business/arts, patriotic stories, instructive items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match story focus to the audience likely to be interested; many stories have more than one kind of news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelve-question checklist for newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of twelve questions to appraise a story's news value: 1) Is it accurate? 2) Is it new? 3) Is it interesting? 4) Is it unusual? 5) Is there an element of contest? 6) Does it have local interest? 7) Does it appeal to the sentiments? 8) Does it tell of loss of life or property? 9) Does it concern prominent persons/well-known places/famous events? 10) Does it appeal to any of the seven personal interests? 11) How many people will it interest and how keen will interest be? 12) How can I present this story to arouse the highest interest and how much am I justified in writing about it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conscientious answers to these questions enable reporters to estimate the worth of stories and to avoid unnecessary information; use as a practical decision tool before filing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity is essential in news writing — 'Not a word should be wasted in writing a newspaper account of an event.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary bits of information; write tightly — 'Brevity is the soul and body of the news story.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and follow the paper's policy and editor's preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper's editorial policy and the personal preferences of editors affect how stories are 'played' (e.g., conservative papers play down sensationalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a story should theoretically stand on its merits, reporters should learn their paper's policies and editors' tastes and observe them to avoid repeated mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use aggravate for irritate or annoy
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'aggravate' when 'irritate' or 'annoy' is meant; 'aggravate' means to add to the weight or severity of something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'I was aggravated by his remarks.' Right: 'I was irritated (or annoyed) by his remarks.' Example: 'The pain was aggravated by his attempt to walk.'

rubrics_metrics.name: As should not be used as a causal connective
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'as' to mean 'because' or 'since' as a causal connective; prefer 'since,' 'for,' or 'because.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak: 'I cannot go, as I am busy.' Better: 'I cannot go, for I am busy.' Also: 'As I was angry, I did not answer.' → 'Because I was angry, I did not answer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Between must not be applied to more than two things; use among for more than two
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'between' only for divisions involving two parties; use 'among' when more than two are involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'We will divide it between the four boys.' Right: 'We will divide it among the four boys.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Canine and feline are adjectives; avoid using them as nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'canine' and 'feline' as nouns to mean 'dog' and 'cat'; they are adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'The canine chased the feline.' Right: 'The dog chased the cat.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'dived' not 'dove' for past tense of dive (in this usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dove' is a noun designating a bird; it is not the past tense of the verb 'to dive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'We dove off the bank.' Right: 'We dived off the bank.'

rubrics_metrics.name: A coat is hung; a murderer is hanged — distinguish 'hung' vs 'hanged'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'hung' for objects and 'hanged' for execution by hanging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'The man was hung in the jail yard.' Right: 'The man was hanged in the jail yard.' A coat is hung in the closet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'limb' for 'leg' when referring to people
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the crudity of using 'limb' to mean a person's leg; 'limb' more properly refers to parts of trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'Her right limb was fractured.' Right: 'Her right leg was fractured.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Partially should not be used for partly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Partially' implies bias or partiality; 'partly' is the correct adverb for 'in part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong: 'He was only partially successful.' Right: 'He was only partly successful.' Also: 'He decided the question partially.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'retire' to mean 'go to bed'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'retire' as a casual synonym for 'go to bed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not good: 'I am worn out and must retire at once.' Better: 'I am worn out and must go to bed at once.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'stop' for 'stay' in certain colloquial contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'stay' rather than 'stop' when meaning temporary lodging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colloquial: 'I shall stop at the hotel tonight.' Right: 'I shall stay at the hotel tonight.'
